title: Fund the Best Projects to Maximise the Final Capital

concept.title: Among the projects you can afford, always do the most profitable one, then re-check what became affordable
body: You have the capital `w` and can complete **at most `k` different projects**. A project needs a minimum capital `c` to start (the money is not spent, it is only a requirement) and gives a **pure profit** `p` that is added to your capital when it is done. Which projects should you choose to end with the **largest capital**? For the projects `(c, p) = (0, 1) (1, 2) (1, 3)`, `k = 2` and `w = 0` the answer is 4: do the first project (capital 1), then the third (capital 4).

At every moment only the projects with `c <= current capital` are *available*, and doing one never makes the others unavailable, it can only make **more** projects available (the capital never decreases). So there is no reason to prefer a smaller profit now: **among the available projects take the one with the largest profit**. The capital after it is the highest possible, so every project that is available under some other choice is also available now. This is an exchange argument over the `k` steps.

body.code:
order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: capital[i])     # by the required capital
heap = []                                               # profits of the available projects (a max-heap)
i = 0
for _ in range(k):
    while i < n and capital[order[i]] <= w:           # projects that became affordable
        heappush(heap, -profit[order[i]]); i += 1
    if not heap: break                                 # nothing affordable
    w -= heappop(heap)                                 # do the most profitable one
print(w)

body: The two data structures work together: a **sorted list** by capital (a pointer moves forward as the capital grows) and a **max-heap** of the available profits. Each project enters the heap once, so the time is O(n log n). The final capital can reach about 3 * 10^13, so 64-bit numbers are needed. This pattern, "unlock items by a threshold, then take the best unlocked one", appears in many scheduling and shopping problems.

statement: You have the capital `w`. There are `n` projects; the project `i` can be started only if your current capital is at least `capital[i]` (the capital is not consumed) and, when finished, adds `profit[i]` to your capital. You may finish at most `k` projects, each at most once. Print the largest capital you can have at the end.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, `k` and `w`: the number of projects, the largest number of projects you may do and your starting capital.
The second line has `n` numbers: the capital each project requires.
The third line has `n` numbers: the pure profit of each project.
outputFormat: Print the largest possible final capital.

examples.note: Do the project with profit 1 (capital 1), then the one with profit 3: 4.
All three can be done in the order 1, 2, 3: capital 6.

hints: A project becomes available when the capital reaches its requirement.
Doing a project never makes other projects unavailable.
Keep the profits of the available projects in a max-heap and take the largest each time.

explanation: The projects are sorted by the required capital; before each of the k steps the newly affordable projects are pushed into a max-heap of profits, and the most profitable one is done.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

from heapq import heappush, heappop

n, k, w = map(int, input().split())
capital = list(map(int, input().split()))
profit = list(map(int, input().split()))

order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: capital[i])
heap = []
i = 0
for _ in range(k):
    while i < n and capital[order[i]] <= w:
        heappush(heap, -profit[order[i]])
        i += 1
    if not heap:
        break
    w -= heappop(heap)
print(w)
